documents.title: Venus rotation and orbit (offline fixture)
documents.publisher: AI Studio offline fixture, not a real publication
documents.text: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once on its axis, measured against the distant stars. It takes about 225 Earth days to orbit the Sun. Venus also spins in the opposite direction to most planets, so on Venus the Sun would rise in the west and set in the east.

documents.title: Sunrise to sunrise on Venus (offline fixture)
documents.publisher: AI Studio offline fixture, not a real publication
documents.text: Because Venus spins backward while it orbits, the time from one sunrise to the next is shorter than its spin: a solar day on Venus lasts about 117 Earth days. Why Venus spins backward is not settled. Proposed explanations include a giant impact early in its history and tides raised by its thick atmosphere.

segments.narration: A day longer than a year?
On Venus, yes. One spin on its axis takes about 243 Earth days, but one trip around the Sun takes only about 225.
And it spins backward compared with most planets, so the Sun would rise in the west.
Here is the twist. Because it spins backward while it orbits, sunrise to sunrise is much shorter: about 117 Earth days.
Why does it spin backward? Nobody knows for sure. A giant impact long ago, or tides from its thick atmosphere, might have flipped it.
So which is longer on Venus, a day or a year? It depends on which day you mean. Follow IFNOVA for more strange science.
